Vets volunteer, build homes for those in need (posted article in comments to avoid readers having to take a survey)

Here's the article text minus the photos in case anyone wants to avoid taking a survey.

During his 38 years on active duty in the army, Lt. Gen. Keith Huber always felt the duty to serve.

He found 70 other veterans also willing and able to serve Sunday: representing all five branches of the military, the veterans joined together in Antioch to help build homes for three families in need through Habitat for Humanity.

The muddy Sunday offered a chance for the veterans to help three families get a little closer to starting fresh in new homes. But it also gave veterans a chance to continue their service after leaving active duty, Huber said.

"The transition out of uniform is really hard. And it's really hard because we search for communities and groups that we can share unconditional trust with, that we're willing to sacrifice and suffer with...and do exactly what we're doing here," said Huber, who retired from the Army in 2013.

"I don't have a clue how to build a house...we can train each other to do anything. And we work as teams, and we support each other. That is the power of our service, and now we want to continue to give back."

That's part of the reason why veteran service organization The Mission Continues wanted to help build these homes, said Marjorie Eastman, platoon leader for the Nashville chapter of the national organization.

With Veterans Day approaching, Eastman said its important for the community to remember veterans want to continue to serve their communities any way that they can.

"Let's show in our month, how we don't want on Nov. 11 the discount at Applebee's. We want to show folks that this is what we're about," Eastman said, paraphrasing a comment she heard from a U.S. Marine who helped organize Sunday's event.

"We don't want a hand, we want to give a hand. This is our legacy, we're a legacy of service."

As is typical on a Habitat for Humanity build, members of the three families receiving the homes participated in the building on Sunday. According to Habitat, the home recipients include:

Adrienne Clark: Clark, raising her goddaughter and niece, lives in a neighborhood where she doesn't feel safe. She's worked as a nurse at St. Thomas Hospital since 2010.

Ibrahim Hassam and Sakino Nor: Originally from Somalia, the couple fled in the midst of the country's civil war. Married with three children, Ibrahim is a truck driver while Sakino stays home to raise their children. Angelo Uyath and Jude Akaro: Both from Sudan, they too came to the U.S. amid fighting in their home country. Married in 2005, the couple has four daughters and can't afford an apartment large enough to accommodate their family.

Sakino said she and her family truly appreciated the help of the veterans and Habitat for Humanity.

This was the fourth weekend of construction on the homes. The homes are set to be completed by Nov. 15.

STAHLHELM: “Well, no. We can’t. They’d try everything to smear us and destroy us, as they always have. It’s never worked, though.”

STEINER: “Exactly. What this is is just more fighting against us by the forces of the international who is totally uninterested in seeing Germany rise or to anything better than ‘mediocre’. These half-truths, misconstructions of facts, and downright lies (in terms of names) only serves to further prove that we are in the right. For in times of universal deceit, telling the truth is a revolutionary act. I, and the DNVP, have committed no wrongs. I will gladly stand trial in the Hague, and I will laugh in the faces of the Dutch when I am found not guilty or otherwise acquitted.”

STAHLHELM: “But what about allegations of corruption and misuse of money?”

STEINER, smiling: “Check our finances records (which are also published on the DNVP’s website, though with any personal data blurred out). There is no discrepancies whatsoever. We, the DNVP, receives up to millions over the years in donations, membership dues, money we have organizing concerts and rock showings for people on the True Right. STAHLHELM: “And as for the allegations of ‘organized crime’?”

STEINER, after a laugh: “Completely ridiculous in every sense of the word. It is nothing more than baseless accusations from people scraping the bottom of a barrel that does not even exist to justify trying to silence me. Everything they’re accusation thereof is just plain silly: they don’t say that what I am doing is ‘crime’, they merely suggest that ‘well, it could be’. Really, look at the allegations yourself. STAHLHELM: “What’s the deal with the WAG in this matter, anyhow?”

STEINER: “I freely admit: getting that whole thing up and running may not have been my proudest moment. I needed a way to keep the Germans in Liberia safe, but also needed to make sure it was all legal and, better yet, could turn a profit. Legally speaking, Die Westafrikagesellschaft has nothing to do with the DNVP other then some capital we officially and quite legally lent Nikolai Kraus, who is technically a former member of ours. “Die WAG is totally independent of us and is a Liberian company, subject only to Liberian laws, not ours. Money we receive from them is payments in return for the loan. STAHLHELM: “No, that about wraps up any questions we had. Thank you for your time, Herr Steiner.”

STEINER, with a genial smile: “Any time. Don’t be a stranger, now. And I’m glad you bothered to ask me to my face. After all, ‘the truth does not fear investigation’, and nor do I.”
